doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Producing Roberta Flack's first album
summary: Rahsaan and Les McCann pointed Dorn to Roberta Flack. He tells of the failed live-audience recording and the redo with Ron Carter and Bill Fischer's strings.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: I was looking at that, I’m a type of person who just thinks it’s so neat when you see Bucky Pizzarelli here and all these musicians who can move from one genre to another, and a producer who can do that too. So when I looked on Robert Flack’s first record and then I see Bucky Pizzarelli and I say now how did he end up on that record?

Simple. The arranger hired him. I never met Bucky. Let me tell you about that first record. Rahsaan had called me up from Washington and he said, “I’ve got a girl singer for you.” I said, “what’s her name?” He said, “Roberta Novosel, she’s married to my bass player, Steve Novosel.” I said okay. And I said to him, “what does she sound like?” And he got mad and he said, “she sounds like a colored lady” and he slammed the phone down, you know? I don’t know what I said, you know, what does she sound like? About a year later — and that was the end of it — about a year later Les McCann calls me, again like seven in the morning, he’d been up all night. He said, “man, I got it, I got the chick” blah blah blah. This is it, you and me. So I said, “cool, what’s her name?” He said, “Roberta Flack.” He said you won’t believe her. So we actually signed her on Les’ say- so. And before — I sent her a contract before I heard her. Then I heard a very rough demo tape that a guy named Tony Taylor had made, which had been sent to all the companies including Atlantic and had been turned down. But we had a halfway hit with Les on “With These Hands,” from the “Much Les” record, it’s the first record I did with him. So I went to Nesuhi and I said, “Les McCann says he has a singer.” He said, “what does she sound like?” I said, “I haven’t heard her,” I said, “but he’s insane.” He said, “well, sign her, you’ve got ten grand” to make the first album, which wasn’t a bad budget in those days. So I signed her. She wanted to make the record with her trio. She’d been playing at a club called Mr. Henry’s in D.C. and she had a working trio. And she wanted to record in front of people who were fans of hers from Washington so they brought a busload of people up, we went to RCA Studios and we made the record and it wasn’t very good. She was great, but her band wasn’t up to it, the audience was conscious that there were mics so they started applauding out of nowhere and yelling. It was ghastly. So I went back to Nesuhi and I said, “look, this girl’s really good but this record isn’t.” I said, “I want to see if she’ll agree to do it again. Can I have another ten thousand?” Can I have another ten thousand dollars Mr. Simpson, you know. So I said, “I want to do it again.” So he was kind enough to say yes. Boy I must have been like Peck’s Bad Boy to him. You know when I think back, some of this stuff he went through. So I got Ron Carter and Ray Lucas, a brilliant drummer, and Roberta and Ron — she and Ron had a really nice thing and he kind of had a lot to do with the ease of the session. Then I had been working with a young arranger named Bill Fischer and I had met him, Joe Zawinul introduced me to him. And I loved the way he wrote strings so I had no budget, so we had money for seven strings and he said, “you should put a guitar in here too,” he said, “I’m going to call Bucky.” So now we had Bucky and the strings, we do the album, it comes out, you know, it sold about a hundred fifty thousand albums in a year, and you know she’s going to be somebody.
